newsitem.title: USA: American pilots doubtful of deal to avoid strike.
newsitem.headline: American pilots doubtful of deal to avoid strike.

text.p: American Airlines pilots' union said on Friday it was not optimistic about averting a strike that would ground the nation's second largest carrier and spoil the busy holiday weekend for thousands of travelers.

As air travelers around the country braced for cancelled flights and long delays over the busy Presidents Day weekend, progress in talks between pilots and the airline was slow with less than 11 hours left until a midnight strike deadline.
"I can't say I'm optimistic at this point," David Bates, a spokesman for the Allied Pilots Association, said after the two sides negotiated through the night with a mediator shuttling between them.
Government mediator Kenneth Hipp said he was somewhat more encouraged by the negotiations but cautioned that major problems remained.

The pilots have set a midnight(0500 GMT Saturday) deadline for an agreement to avert a strike that would shut down the airline, which carries about 20 percent of the nation's air travelers and could cost the economy $200 million a day.
As the prospect of a strike grew, pressure increased on President Bill Clinton to act, but the White House refused to discuss possible presidential intervention in the dispute.
The president, who has been keeping a close eye on the negotiations, again urged the airline and the union to work out a solution.
"They need to go back to work. They have a few more hours of work to do," Clinton said, looking at his watch, after a reporter asked if he would intervene to avert a strike.
Clinton could create a special emergency board to forge a compromise, which would prevent a work stoppage for 60 days while the deal was drawn up and considered by both sides.
Fort Worth, Texas-based American has 2,200 flights that carry about 200,000 passengers a day.
Sen. Kay Bailey Hutchison, a Republican from Texas, urged President Clinton to step in if necessary.

"I've urged him to look at the powers he has and to see what the impact is on our area of the country and several other areas of the country and be ready to kick in, if something doesn't happen today," she said on CNN.
The dispute put Clinton in a tough position because organised labour is a key supporter of his Democratic Party.
"We never agree with taking the strike weapon out of the hands of workers," said an American Federation of Labour official, when asked how the unions would view intervention.
The key issues in the talks are pay for pilots flying big jets, and whether members of the Allied Pilots Association should fly smaller jets for American's commuter carrier, American Eagle.
American has said it needs to fly the new, small jets with lower-paid pilots from another union if it is to compete with other major carriers offering low-cost commuter flights.

Brian Mayhew, the pilots' chief negotiator, said on Thursday the pilots had offered a new proposal on pay -- presumably less than the 11.5 percent pay increase over four years sought earlier -- but gave no details. The latest offer from American was a 6 percent raise over four years.
With the strike deadline looming, American Airlines spokesman Chris Chiames Friday declined to comment on details of the talks except to say "it's a dynamic situation."
"I'm not going to confirm any of the details about the status or the type of negotiations," Chiames said, adding American had not rejected union demands.
"If something has not been accepted it does not mean it has been rejected," he said.
Chiames appeared to be responding to union statements on Thursday night that American had rejected the latest offer from the pilots aimed at settling the dispute.
The stock of AMR Corp., American's parent company, fell $1.50 to $81.625 on the New York Stock Exchange.
